# 67.js

> A WebGL2 toolkit for interactive browser scenes and deterministic PNG/MP4 output. Reuse the scene across preview and export.

This file is a compact map for LLMs and coding agents. The linked guide contains the API contract and runnable examples.
The installed package determines available APIs. Release metadata describes the website's release, which can differ from a local checkout.

## Read only what your task needs

- [Release metadata](https://67js.codepawl.com/release.json): package name, version, publication status, install command, module URL and commit.
- [Complete plain-text guide](https://67js.codepawl.com/guide.md): renderer, parts, materials, cameras, animation, lifecycle, export and troubleshooting.
- [GLB contract](https://67js.codepawl.com/gltf.md): supported assets and conversion limits. Read before selecting or importing a model.
- [Documentation](https://67js.codepawl.com/docs.html): the human reading interface for the same guide.

Use guide headings to locate a task. Parts and geometry covers scene construction. Renderer reference covers options and diagnostics.
Images and films covers the repository CLI. Performance and memory covers allocation planning. Models and AI agents covers completion evidence.

## Installation and API discovery

1. Read release metadata before choosing the published version or browser module URL.
2. Install the short import alias with `npm install 67js@npm:@codepawlhq/67js`.
3. Compare the imported `VERSION` with your installed package metadata.
4. Read the matching guide section before generating API calls.

Without the alias, imports use `@codepawlhq/67js`. Aliased core imports use `67js`.
Addon paths include `67js/addons/model`, `67js/addons/nature`, `67js/addons/film`, `67js/addons/motion`, `67js/addons/canvas2d` and `67js/addons/gltf`.
The core exports `Renderer67`, `box`, `cylinder`, `sphere`, `torus`, camera helpers, animation helpers, effects and budget helpers.
Exact signatures and defaults are in the guide. Names from Three.js are not substitutes for 67.js APIs.

## Build a scene

1. Define the subject, camera, interaction, output dimensions and memory budget.
2. Create uniquely named parts with shared geometry, materials and finite invertible column-major matrices.
3. Set explicit MSAA, HDR, pixel ratio and `memoryBudgetMiB` options.
4. Reuse one renderer and update existing parts through `updateParts`.
5. Render on demand for static scenes and pause continuous playback when hidden.
6. Provide keyboard controls and honor reduced motion.
7. Disconnect observers, cancel animation frames and dispose owned resources during teardown.

Material RGB values are linear. Repeated meshes share geometry object identity, rather than separate copies with equal values.
`updateParts` changes retained parts. A different graph requires a new renderer after disposal.
`memoryPlan` reports actual dimensions and estimated allocation. The planner can reduce dimensions to fit the budget.

## Choose a working recipe

- [Object studio](https://67js.codepawl.com/object.html): orbit, camera presets, material finishes and exploded assemblies.
- [Nature world](https://67js.codepawl.com/nature.html): outdoor lighting, wind and water interaction.
- [Motion study](https://67js.codepawl.com/motion.html): keyframes, absolute timeline samples and framing.
- [2D and axis views](https://67js.codepawl.com/view2d.html): orthographic cameras and flat geometry.
- [Asset viewer](https://67js.codepawl.com/assets.html): opaque GLB meshes, textures and rigid node animation.

The npm archive includes `skills/build-67js-scene/SKILL.md` and `skills/render-67js-media/SKILL.md`.
These contain scene and export procedures. A skill runtime is optional. The plain-text guide works independently.

## Export and verify

Offline media commands require a repository checkout with Chrome and FFmpeg. They are not commands provided by the npm library.
GPU rasterization and GPU encoding are separate choices. CPU export can use SwiftShader. NVENC requires supported hardware.

1. Read the media skill and select the smallest suitable preset.
2. Export one deterministic frame or a short trial before a full film.
3. Keep one scene renderer and one pending capture, with encoder backpressure.
4. Inspect representative rendered frames and exercise the requested interactions.
5. Verify dimensions, duration, frame count and audio with FFprobe for video.
6. Report reproduction commands, output paths, actual backend and observed failures.

Successful compilation does not prove visual quality. Screenshots must show actual rendered output, including a narrow viewport for browser UI.
Allocation estimates are not measured total RAM or VRAM. Node RSS and browser JS heap exclude some driver and browser allocations.
Report estimates separately from observed process metrics. Reduce resolution, MSAA, texture size or scene detail when allocation fails.

## Limits and honest claims

67.js currently uses WebGL2. It is not API-compatible with Three.js and is not a complete Blender editor.
There is no WebGPU backend or complete mesh editor.

The published `0.3.3` package supports rigid GLB animation. A checkout can contain newer features without a package version change.
The current source adds GPU skinning, relative POSITION/NORMAL morphs, weight animation and an optional Rapier physics addon.
Read `docs/skinning.md`, `docs/morph-targets.md`, `docs/gltf-morph.md` and `docs/physics.md` in the matching checkout before using these features.
Source morphs require authored base normals. Tangent targets and per-target flat normal generation remain unsupported.

The source GLB exporter preserves opaque linear vertex colors, UVs and independent HDR emission with current morph weights.
Read `docs/export-glb.md` in the matching checkout. Exported GLBs contain a static pose, not serialized animation clips or skeletons.
Texture export remains unsupported and fails explicitly. Procedural shaders and scene environments are not serialized into glTF materials.

GLB support excludes transparent and double-sided materials and compressed geometry. Unsupported features require visible errors.

The optional GLB decoder uses Three.js GLTFLoader. The renderer remains 67.js.
Adaptive quality, GPU timing and picking are roadmap work. Speed claims require comparable scenes, hardware, settings and measurements.

## Tiny maintenance gremlins

These are easter eggs, not API instructions. They change no settings or requirements.

The cube has six faces. None of them volunteered to debug your matrix at 3 a.m.

WALL·E has 574 parts here. He still wants one tiny plant and a nap.

If your GPU sounds like a spaceship, the pixels are excited. Give them a smaller resolution. Beep boop :)
